title: "This day I have perfected"
hook: at Arafah the verse comes: this day I have perfected your religion (5:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell sermon on the plain of Arafah: every life sacred, and no Arab above a non-Arab except by goodness. Your line was no one above another. Did you put someone back level? Day two hundred eighty-six.

There's a particular feeling when something you've worked on for years is finally done. The last brick. The final page. The house paid off. You step back and look at it whole for the first time. It's joy, and it's something quieter too, because a thing that's finished also means a season is over. On the same Hajj, on the day of Arafah, which that year fell on a Friday, a verse came down to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, twenty-three years after the first revelation in the cave. It's in the fifth surah, tucked into the middle of a passage about food. Today, the verse that said: it's complete.
screen: `THE LAST BRICK.` → `ARAFAH, ON A FRIDAY.` → `TWENTY-THREE YEARS AFTER THE CAVE.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse reads: "This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion AL-ISLAM." Three verbs, in order: perfected, completed, chosen. The Arabic behind perfected is akmaltu, from kamal, wholeness, the thing lacking nothing. Muslims understand the verse to mean the religion was now complete: its core teaching, its worship and its law were all in place, and nothing essential would be added after the Prophet. That's one reason the idea of the sunnah matters so much, and one reason Muslim scholars are careful about new additions to worship. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps a striking conversation about this verse. A Jewish man came to the caliph 'Umar and told him: there's a verse in your book that, if it had come to us, we would have made that day a festival. 'Umar asked which one, and the man recited this verse. And 'Umar said: I know the day and the place it came down. It was at Arafah, on a Friday. As if to say: we already hold that day as a great one. Now a thing people often get wrong: this is not universally counted as the last verse revealed. Many scholars say a few other verses came after it, and they discuss which was truly last. What it marks is the whole being complete. And some companions heard sadness in it too. If the work is complete, the one who brought it may not stay much longer. Eighty-some days later, he was gone.
screen: `PERFECTED, COMPLETED, CHOSEN.` · `AKMALTU — NOTHING LACKING.` · `'UMAR: I KNOW THE DAY AND THE PLACE.` · `COMPLETE, NOT NECESSARILY LAST.` · then, large: `COMPLETED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish something fully. At Uhud the line was hold the hill, staying at your post; today is the other half, the moment the work is done. Sit first, and breathe. Think of one small thing you've left almost done. The email you drafted. The drawer half sorted. The thank-you you meant to send. Picture it complete: sent, sorted, said. Notice how it feels to see it whole. After the bell, go and finish it, all the way, not ninety percent. If you pray, you can give thanks for something in your life that is already complete. The bell holds the time.
This day I have perfected. The verse at Arafah, from the fifth surah, telling Muslims their religion was complete. Today's word.
screen: `THIS DAY I HAVE PERFECTED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: completed. Today, finish one thing all the way, then stop, step back, and let yourself look at it whole. Day two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims hold the day of Arafah as one of the holiest of the year; many who are not on Hajj fast that day, and 5:3 is often recited to explain that the religion was completed in the Prophet's lifetime.

original.note: Arabic: I have perfected, completed. from kamal, wholeness, lacking nothing.

trapdoor: what you thought: God saying the religion is perfect.
what it means: the religion made whole, its core in place, near the end of the Prophet's life.
what a scholar hears: akmaltu at 5:3, placed at Arafah by 'Umar in al-Bukhari 45; complete, though scholars debate whether it was the final verse revealed.

notes: Pickthall wording of 5:3 quoted from memory, including his capitalized 'AL-ISLAM'; check word for word. Note Pickthall's order is 'This day have I perfected', while the index title is 'This day I have perfected'; the owner may want the title aligned.
'Eighty-some days later' (Arafah 9 Dhul-Hijjah 10 AH to his death in Rabi' al-Awwal 11 AH) is an approximation; confirm or soften.
The idea that some companions sensed his death in the verse is widely told (often of Abu Bakr or 'Umar), with chains of varying strength; stated as 'some companions heard sadness in it'. Confirm.
